worksheet.title: Two Scripts, One Event
worksheet.subtitle: The same event starts both scripts
worksheet.learning_goal: I can read two scripts that the same event starts at the same time.

parts.title: One event, two scripts
parts.text: Bit (green) and Pixel (purple) each have their own script. Look at the top of each one — they BOTH start with 'when green flag clicked'. So ONE click of the green flag starts BOTH scripts at the SAME time. Two scripts running together are called parallel scripts. Each sprite moves from its own home.

parts.title: Where does Bit land?
parts.prompt: The green flag is clicked. Bit's script runs from home 0: forward 2. What number does Bit land on?

parts.title: Where does Pixel land?
parts.prompt: The same green flag also starts Pixel's script from home 5: back 1. What number does Pixel land on?

parts.title: One event, both at once
parts.prompt: How many times did you click the green flag to start BOTH scripts? Write the number. Then write where each lands. Bit: ____  Pixel: ____

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: When two scripts share the same event hat, ONE event starts them both — they run in parallel. You only click the green flag once, and both Bit and Pixel go at the same time, each on its own script.

teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key
teacher_guide.footer_topic: 2. Two Scripts, One Event — Teacher Guide

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students see PARALLEL SCRIPTS: two scripts that share the same event hat ('when green flag clicked') both start from one event and run at the same time. The key idea is that one event can trigger more than one script — a single green-flag click launches both Bit and Pixel. Reading and running parallel (concurrent) scripts is the Grade-2 C3.1 idea.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum (Grade 2 — C3 Coding)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: The printed worksheet and a pencil. Optional: two counters (green Bit, purple Pixel) on a 0-5 floor path; hold up ONE 'green flag' card and move BOTH counters at once to show one event starting two scripts.

parts.title: Run it (about 20 min)
text: 1. I DO: point to the top block of EACH script — both say 'when green flag clicked'. 'Same event on both means one click starts both.'
2. WE DO: trace Bit (0 forward 2 → 2) and Pixel (5 back 1 → 4) after one flag click.
3. YOU DO: students answer both landings and that only ONE click was needed to start both.
4. Connect: 'One event, two scripts — that is parallel.'

parts.title: Answer key (modelled by the run-gate)
text: Ex 1 — Bit: 0 → forward 2 → 2. Bit lands on 2.
Ex 2 — Pixel: 5 → back 1 → 4. Pixel lands on 4.
Ex 3 — ONE green-flag click starts both (the same event sits on top of both scripts). Bit lands on 2, Pixel on 4.
Event note: the single green-flag event triggers both hat blocks, so the two scripts run in parallel from that one event.

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common error: thinking you need to click the flag twice (once per script) — one event triggers every script with that hat.
Common error: running one script fully, then the other — they start together from the one event (parallel).
Simplify: cover Pixel, run Bit; then reveal Pixel and show the SAME flag starts it too.
Extend: ask what happens if only Bit had the green-flag hat and Pixel had none (only Bit would run).
Success indicator: the child lands Bit on 2 and Pixel on 4 and says one click started both.
